In the dry AMD context this assay models key aspects of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) energy failure under chronic oxidative or lipofuscin‐mediated stress.  
•  Disease aspect modeled: mitochondrial dysfunction and compensatory glycolytic shift in RPE, central to RPE atrophy and photoreceptor degeneration in dry AMD.  
•  Measurements:  
   – Basal OCR (ATP‐linked respiration), maximal respiration (FCCP‐stimulated), proton leak, spare respiratory capacity.  
   – Basal ECAR and glycolytic capacity (glucose, oligomycin, 2-DG injections).  
   – Data acquired via fluorescent oxygen and pH sensors in the Seahorse XF cartridge.  
•  Biological material: primary human RPE (fetal or adult donor), iPSC-derived RPE, or ARPE-19 cells preconditioned with chronic oxidative stress (e.g., H₂O₂, A2E) or lipofuscin to mimic aged RPE.  

Biomedical Evidence  
1.  Mitochondrial dysfunction is an early and central event in dry AMD pathogenesis:  
    – Postmortem AMD RPE mitochondria show reduced complex I/III activities and altered morphology (Ferrington et al., Sci Rep. 2018; Ferrington et al., J Proteome Res. 2017).  
    – Genetic and transcriptomic studies link AMD risk alleles (CFH, ARMS2/HTRA1) to impaired RPE mitochondrial homeostasis and oxidative‐stress responses (Ratnapriya et al., Nature Genet. 2019).  
2.  Energy imbalance contributes to drusen formation and RPE atrophy:  
    – Under oxidative or A2E‐induced stress, RPE shifts toward glycolysis but fails to meet ATP demand, triggering inflammasome activation and cell death (Saini et al., Aging Cell. 2017; Estner et al., IOVS. 2019).  
    – Clinical imaging (OCT, FAF) correlates regions of metabolic stress with geographic atrophy progression (Smith et al., Prog Retin Eye Res. 2019).  
3.  Restoring mitochondrial function protects RPE:  
    – Activation of PGC-1α or treatments that boost NAD⁺ levels rescue mitochondrial respiration, reduce ROS, and delay RPE senescence (Zhang et al., Aging Cell. 2015; Terluk et al., Mol Vis. 2015).  

Previous Use  
•  Drug discovery:  
   – Seahorse profiling has been used to screen small molecules (PGC-1α agonists, NAD⁺ precursors) in oxidatively stressed ARPE-19 or iPSC-RPE to identify compounds that restore spare respiratory capacity (Fisher et al., Redox Biol. 2019).  
   – A2E-treated primary RPE were assayed to reveal that antioxidants (e.g., MitoQ) normalize ΔΨm and OCR, guiding preclinical validation (Chakrabarti et al., Free Radic Biol Med. 2016).  
•  Mechanistic insights:  
   – Demonstrated that RPE under lipofuscin‐mediated photooxidative stress exhibit a “metabolic bottleneck” at complex II, later linked to impaired mitophagy (Dunaief et al., Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci. 2016).  
   – Identified that ETC flux deficits precede lysosomal alkalinization and drusen-like deposit formation in 3D RPE cultures (Sokol et al., Autophagy. 2018).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths:  
•  Direct functional readout of two core energy pathways, highly relevant to dry AMD RPE pathology.  
•  Quantitative, kinetics‐based, amenable to medium-throughput screening of therapeutic libraries (96-well format).  
•  Sensitive to partial rescue of mitochondrial reserve, enabling early go/no‐go decisions in lead optimization.  

Weaknesses:  
•  Monoculture RPE lacks Bruch’s membrane, photoreceptors, immune components—limits modeling of drusen formation and para-inflammatory milieu.  
•  Seahorse assays require careful optimization of cell density, medium buffering, and stress paradigms; inter-batch variability can challenge reproducibility.  
•  OCR/ECAR changes may reflect general cytotoxicity or off-target metabolic effects, necessitating orthogonal validation (e.g., ATP assays, ROS measurements, mitophagy markers).  

Conclusion  
The Seahorse XF Metabolic Flux Assay provides a robust, disease-relevant readout of RPE energy dysfunction in dry AMD. Its ability to quantify mitochondrial and glycolytic parameters under controlled stress makes it a powerful tool for early-stage screening of compounds aimed at preserving RPE bioenergetics. However, hits must be validated in more complex co-culture or organoid models to ensure translation to in vivo AMD pathology.', 'index': '12'}

• Assay principle and disease modeling  
 – Measure lysosomal pH in live retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells using pH‐sensitive fluorescent probes (LysoTracker Green DND-26 or pHrodo Red dextran).  
 – Model the key dry AMD pathogenic cascade in which photo-oxidized RPE lipofuscin pigments (notably A2E) accumulate, raise lysosomal pH, impair degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), autophagy, and promote RPE dysfunction.  
• Readouts and methodology  
 – Cells are incubated with A2E (or lipofuscin‐like pigments) for 24–72 h to induce lysosomal alkalinization.  
 – Following compound treatment, LysoTracker (accumulates in acidic vesicles) or pHrodo (fluorescence increases with acidification) is added.  
 – Quantify probe fluorescence by high‐content imaging or flow cytometry; optionally use ratiometric pH standards to convert fluorescence to absolute pH values.  
 – Secondary end points: co-staining for LAMP1/LC3 to assess lysosomal/autophagic flux, measurement of cellular A2E content (HPLC or fluorescence).  
• Cell system  
 – Human ARPE-19 or primary human fetal RPE monolayers, or iPSC-derived RPE differentiated for ≥4 weeks.  
 – Optionally co-culture with POS to recapitulate phagocytic load.

• Centrality of lysosomal acidification to dry AMD  
 – Clinical hallmark: drusen deposition and RPE atrophy, preceded by lipofuscin accumulation and POS–lysosome fusion defects (Sarks et al. IOVS 2007; Ferrington et al. Prog Retin Eye Res 2016).  
 – A2E, a major fluorophore of lipofuscin, raises lysosomal pH by interfering with vacuolar ATPase, hindering enzyme activity (Yao et al. J Biol Chem 2005).  
 – Elevated lysosomal pH blocks autophagy and POS degradation, escalating chronic inflammation and complement activation in RPE (Mitter et al. Nat Commun 2014).  
 – Postmortem AMD eyes show reduced cathepsin activity and altered lysosomal marker expression (Nashine et al. Exp Eye Res 2015).  
• Clinical linkage  
 – Patients with early dry AMD exhibit fundus autofluorescence correlated with lipofuscin load; autofluorescence intensity predicts progression to geographic atrophy (Delori et al. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2011).  
 – No approved therapies for dry AMD; restoring lysosomal/autophagic function is recognized as a promising therapeutic avenue (Khandhadia & Lotery. Br J Ophthalmol 2010).

• Discovery and validation studies  
 – Sparrow and colleagues (IOVS 2008, 2010) used LysoTracker in ARPE-19 cells loaded with A2E to screen small-molecule acidotropic agents that re-acidify lysosomes. They demonstrated that certain polyenals lower pH and reduce A2E accumulation.  
 – Mitter et al. (Autophagy 2012) applied pHrodo dextran to show that rapamycin-mediated autophagy induction restored lysosomal acidity and enhanced POS clearance in stressed RPE.  
• High-throughput adaptation  
 – Several groups have optimized 96- and 384-well plate formats with automated confocal imaging to screen libraries of FDA-approved compounds for lysosomal pH–lowering activity (Zhang et al. SLAS Discov 2015).  
• Key discoveries  
 – Identification of v-ATPase modulators that reverse A2E-induced alkalinization and reduce lipofuscin load (Sparrow et al. Chem Biol 2011).  
 – Link between lysosomal pH correction and decreased complement factor secretion by RPE, suggesting anti-inflammatory potential (Mitter et al. JCI Insight 2017).

Strengths  
• Disease relevance: Directly models a mechanistic node—lysosomal alkalinization—strongly implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis.  
• Quantitative, live-cell, high-throughput–compatible readouts allow screening of diverse compound libraries.  
• Multiplexable: can combine with autophagy, oxidative stress, complement activation assays for mechanistic profiling.  
• Use of human RPE (primary or iPSC-derived) enhances translational value.

• Cell model limitations: ARPE-19 cells may not fully mimic mature RPE; primary/iPSC-derived RPE require lengthy differentiation and batch validation.  
• Artificial A2E loading may not recapitulate in vivo lipofuscin composition or accumulation kinetics.  
• Lysosomal probes (LysoTracker) can bind nonspecifically in off-target acidic compartments; careful calibration and controls are essential.  
• Altering lysosomal pH in vitro does not guarantee functional rescue of complex in vivo processes (e.g., Bruch’s membrane turnover, choroidal blood flow).  
• Potential assay interference from autofluorescent or colored test compounds.

The lysosomal pH assay in live RPE provides a robust, disease-mechanistic platform to identify and rank compounds that reverse A2E-induced lysosomal dysfunction—a central driver of dry AMD. The mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) assay uses potentiometric dyes (JC-1 or tetramethylrhodamine methyl ester, TMRM) to quantify early mitochondrial dysfunction in live retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells under oxidative stress. In practice:  
• Cells: Human RPE cell lines (ARPE-19) or primary RPE from donor eyes.  
• Stressor: Sublethal hydrogen peroxide (100–200 μM) or blue-light irradiation to mimic cumulative oxidative insult seen in dry AMD.  
• Measurement: After treatment with test compounds, cells are incubated with JC-1 (5 µg/mL) or TMRM (25 nM).  
  – JC-1 aggregates in healthy mitochondria (emits red fluorescence) vs. monomers in depolarized mitochondria (green). The red/green fluorescence ratio is quantified by flow cytometry or high-content imaging.  
  – TMRM accumulates in polarized mitochondria; absolute fluorescence intensity correlates with ΔΨm and is recorded by microplate reader or confocal microscopy.  

Biomedical Evidence  
Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis:  
• Clinical correlation: Post-mortem RPE from AMD patients shows fragmented mitochondria, reduced mitochondrial DNA copy number, and decreased electron transport chain activity (Feher et al., Exp. Eye Res. 2006; Golestaneh et al., Invest. Ophth. Vis. Sci. 2017).  
• Oxidative stress link: Chronic light exposure and lipofuscin accumulation in RPE promote reactive oxygen species that impair ΔΨm, triggering RPE apoptosis and subretinal drusen formation (Ferrington et al., Prog. Retin. Eye Res. 2016).  
• Animal models: Mice with RPE-targeted deletion of mitochondrial DNA replication factor Twinkle develop RPE degeneration resembling geographic atrophy (Hanus et al., Free Radic. Biol. Med. 2015).  

Thus, stabilizing ΔΨm in RPE is directly relevant to interrupting RPE dysfunction that precipitates dry AMD.  

Previous Use  
• Early screens: MitoQ and SS-31, two mitochondria-targeted antioxidants, were first validated in ARPE-19 cells by monitoring JC-1 ratios under H₂O₂ stress (Liu et al., Redox Biol. 2017). Protection of ΔΨm correlated with reduced caspase-3 activation.  
• Mechanistic insights: Using TMRM, studies have shown that tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) restores ΔΨm and reduces ER stress in RPE (Castro et al., Mitochondrion. 2013).  
• High-throughput adaptation: Automated high-content screening of small-molecule libraries in 384-well format has been reported, with ΔΨm as an early endpoint for compound selection (Lin et al., J. Biomol. Screen. 2018).  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Pathophysiological relevance: Directly quantifies a central feature of RPE degeneration in dry AMD.  
• Early, sensitive readout: ΔΨm collapse precedes cell death, enabling detection of sub-lethal rescue.  
• Throughput and adaptability: Amenable to plate-based screening and multiplexing with ROS or cell-viability assays.  

Weaknesses  
• In vitro simplification: Lacks Bruch’s membrane, inflammatory milieu, and photoreceptor interactions integral to dry AMD.  
• Probe limitations: JC-1 aggregation can be affected by cell density and non-mitochondrial binding; TMRM requires careful calibration to avoid quenching.  
• Translational gap: Rescue of ΔΨm in RPE may not predict functional preservation of photoreceptors or clinical endpoints such as geographic atrophy progression.  

Conclusion  
A ΔΨm assay in RPE provides a mechanistically grounded, quantifiable platform to identify mitochondrial-stabilizing therapeutics for dry AMD. It is most powerful when combined with complementary assays (e.g., oxidative stress markers, inflammasome activation) and ultimately followed by co-culture or ex-vivo models to address tissue-level complexity.', 'index': '2'}

{'hypothesis': 'Nrf2-ARE Reporter Assay', 'answer': 'Assay Overview  
• Goal: Quantify activation of the Nrf2–antioxidant response element (ARE) pathway in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells as a surrogate for induction of cytoprotective phase II enzymes.  
• What is modeled: Oxidative‐injury defense in RPE, a key node in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) pathogenesis. RPE in AMD is chronically exposed to reactive oxygen species (ROS) from photo‐oxidation, lipofuscin accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction.  
• Readout: Luminescence signal from an integrated ARE‐driven firefly luciferase reporter. Signal increases in proportion to nuclear translocation of Nrf2 and binding to ARE sequences. Optionally, secondary readouts such as ROS levels (e.g., DCFDA fluorescence), phase II enzyme mRNA (qPCR for NQO1/HO-1), or cell viability (MTT or ATP assays) can be run in parallel.  
• Biological material: Human RPE cell line (e.g., ARPE-19 or hTERT–RPE1) stably transfected with a reporter plasmid containing tandem repeats of the consensus ARE upstream of luciferase. Primary human RPE could be used for validation but is less amenable to stable reporter integration.  

Biomedical Evidence  
• Central role of oxidative stress in dry AMD: Numerous clinical studies have shown elevated markers of lipid peroxidation (e.g., malondialdehyde) and protein oxidative damage in AMD donor eyes. Oxidative injury to RPE leads to drusen formation, complement activation, and cell death.  
• Nrf2 impairment in AMD: Postmortem RPE from dry AMD patients exhibit reduced nuclear Nrf2 staining and diminished expression of Nrf2 target genes (NQO1, GCLM, HO-1). Animal models: Nrf2⁻/⁻ mice develop age‐related RPE degeneration, drusen‐like deposits, and complement upregulation.  
• Clinical relevance: Polymorphisms in NFE2L2 (the gene encoding Nrf2) have been linked to AMD susceptibility in several cohorts. Nutritional trials (AREDS, AREDS2) demonstrated that antioxidants slow progression, indirectly supporting the strategy of bolstering endogenous detox pathways.  

Previous Use  
• Drug discovery: Nrf2–ARE reporter assays have been extensively used to screen libraries for oxidative‐stress modulators. In hepatic, neuronal and RPE‐derived reporter lines, hits include electrophilic phytochemicals and synthetic triterpenoids.  
• Key findings in RPE: Nguyen et al. (Mol Cell Biol 2009) established the reporter concept; subsequent RPE‐specific screens identified compounds that both increased ARE‐luciferase activity and conferred protection against H₂O₂‐induced cell death. Some hits were shown to upregulate HO-1 and NQO1 in RPE and reduce ROS accumulation.  
• Translational impact: A subset of Nrf2 activators discovered via similar reporter screens advanced to animal models of retinal oxidative injury and, in some cases, to early‐phase clinical testing for ocular protection.  

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
• Disease relevance: Models the oxidative‐stress axis central to dry AMD pathogenesis. Directly reads out induction of endogenous cytoprotective machinery rather than an indirect proxy.  
• Quantitative and high‐throughput: Luciferase assays are robust, sensitive (signal-to-noise >100-fold) and scalable for 96- or 384-well formats, enabling rapid SAR and dose–response studies.  
• Flexibility: Can be paired with secondary assays (ROS, cytokine release, complement factor expression) to build multi‐parametric profiles of hit compounds.  

Weaknesses  
• Pathway focus is narrow: AMD pathogenesis also involves inflammation (complement activation), lipid dysregulation and mitochondrial impairment. Nrf2 activation alone may not predict efficacy on those axes.  
• Artificial reporter context: Overexpression of a multi‐copy ARE element may exaggerate small effects on native promoter occupancy or fail to recapitulate chromatin context.  
• Cell‐line limitations: ARPE-19 cells differ from primary RPE in polarization, melanin content and tight junction fidelity; responses to Nrf2 induction may not fully mirror in vivo RPE behavior.  
• Potential off-target effects: Some electrophilic Nrf2 activators have broad reactivity and may elicit stress responses unrelated to physiological pathway activation, confounding interpretation.  

Conclusion  
The Nrf2–ARE reporter assay in RPE cells is a well‐validated, sensitive platform for identifying compounds that enhance the oxidative‐stress defenses implicated in dry AMD. Its main value lies in early‐stage screening and mechanistic deconvolution of hit compounds’ ability to engage a clinically relevant cytoprotective pathway. However, given the multifactorial nature of AMD, hits should be triaged through complementary assays addressing inflammation, lipofuscin handling and mitochondrial health before advancement.', 'index': '5'}

• Disease aspect modeled: Impaired autophagic clearance in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), a core feature of dry AMD pathogenesis leading to lipofuscin/A2E accumulation, oxidative stress, and eventual RPE cell death.  
• Readouts: Transgenic RPE monolayers (primary human RPE or ARPE-19) stably expressing an mCherry-GFP-LC3 tandem reporter. Under baseline or drug-treated conditions, high-content fluorescence imaging yields:  
  – Number of yellow puncta (mCherry+GFP+; autophagosomes)

  – Autophagic flux score = ratio of red-only to total puncta, or changes in flux over time

• Central role of autophagy in RPE homeostasis: Several groups (Mitter et al. Autophagy 2014; Krohne et al. Exp Eye Res 2010; Ferrington et al. Oxid Med Cell Longev 2016) have shown that chronic light/oxidative stress and bisretinoid buildup (A2E, lipofuscin) impair autophagosome formation and clearance in RPE.  
• Link to dry AMD: Post-mortem human AMD donor eyes exhibit reduced expression of ATG genes (ATG5, ATG7) and lysosomal enzymes (cathepsin D) in the RPE (Zhao et al. Cell Death Differ 2011). • Clinical correlations: Levels of autophagy markers (LC3-II, p62) in the aqueous humor of patients with early AMD differ from controls, suggesting autophagic dysfunction correlates with disease stage (Shi et al. Sci Rep 2015). Enhancing autophagy in RPE reduces lipofuscin accumulation in vitro and in vivo, improving visual function in rodent AMD models (Sinha et al. J Biol Chem 2018).

• Drug discovery: High-content screens using mCherry-GFP-LC3 RPE cells have identified rapamycin analogs, AMPK activators (AICAR), and transcription factor EB (TFEB) agonists as autophagy enhancers that reduce A2E-induced toxicity (Mitter et al. Autophagy 2014; Zhong et al. Nat Commun 2016).  
• Key findings:  
  – Demonstration that trehalose rescues dysfunctional autophagy in A2E-loaded RPE (Wang et al. Sci Rep 2019).  
  – Validation that small-molecule enhancers of lysosomal biogenesis (via TFEB) decrease lipofuscin in RPE and slow photoreceptor degeneration in murine AMD models (Xing et al. EMBO Mol Med 2019).  
• Adaptations: Some studies have combined the reporter assay with co-culture of RPE and macrophages to model drusen clearance and inflammatory crosstalk (Rohrer et al. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2013).

Strengths  
1. Direct, quantitative measure of autophagic flux rather than static LC3 levels.  
2. Scalable to moderate-high throughput 96/384-well formats for screening libraries.  
3. Demonstrated correlation between restored flux and reduction of lipofuscin/A2E toxicity in RPE.  
4. Amenable to multiplexing with viability, reactive oxygen species, or lysosomal pH dyes.

1. Overexpressed reporter may not fully recapitulate endogenous LC3 dynamics; risk of artifactual puncta.  
2. ARPE-19 cells can differ from primary human RPE in autophagic competence and polarization; primary cells are more physiologically relevant but less scalable.  
3. Autophagy modulation is pleiotropic; flux increase may not translate to clinical benefit if downstream lysosomal function remains impaired.  
4. Assay does not model subretinal environment, Bruch’s membrane changes, or immune/inflammatory contributions to dry AMD.

The mCherry-GFP-LC3 autophagic flux assay in RPE monolayers provides a robust, quantitative platform to screen for small molecules that restore autophagy—a mechanism strongly implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. {'hypothesis': 'Tight-Junction Imaging Assay', 'answer': 'Assay Overview  
The Tight-Junction Imaging Assay is a high-content, cell-based readout of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) barrier integrity.  In dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), early RPE dysfunction and loss of the outer blood–retinal barrier are thought to contribute to drusen formation, chronic inflammation, and eventual photoreceptor loss.  In this assay:  
• Cell model:  Primary human RPE, iPSC-derived RPE, or ARPE-19 monolayers are cultured to tight confluence (typically on Transwell inserts or glass-bottom plates).  
• Induced stress:  Cells may be exposed to sublethal oxidative stress (e.g., H2O2 or t-butyl hydroperoxide) or inflammatory mediators (e.g., complement C3a/C5a fragments) to model early AMD-like barrier disruption.  
• Readout:  Immunofluorescent staining for tight-junction markers—ZO-1 (TJP1) and occludin—followed by automated high-content confocal imaging.  Image analysis algorithms quantify junctional belt continuity (percent closed junction perimeter), mean junctional fluorescence intensity, and gap frequency per field.  
• Throughput:  Medium-throughput (96- to 384-well format), compatible with automated liquid handling and image analysis pipelines.  

Biomedical Evidence  
1. RPE barrier breakdown is one of the earliest morphological changes in dry AMD.  Postmortem histology of AMD donor eyes shows discontinuous ZO-1 staining along the apical RPE in areas overlying drusen (Luk et al., Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2015), and electron microscopy reveals widened intercellular spaces preceding frank atrophy.  
2. Genetic and clinical studies implicate chronic low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress as drivers of RPE tight-junction disruption.  Complement activation fragments (C3a, C5a) accumulate locally beneath the RPE and have been shown in vitro to reduce TEER and mislocalize occludin (Chen et al., J Biol Chem 2014).  
3. In iPSC-RPE lines derived from AMD patients, baseline trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) is lower and ZO-1 belts are less continuous than in age-matched controls (Kanda et al., Stem Cells Transl Med 2016), linking RPE barrier integrity to genetic risk and disease phenotype.  
4. Clinically, optical coherence tomography (OCT) of early dry AMD often demonstrates sub-RPE drusenoid deposits and subtle fluid pockets that correlate with barrier compromise.  Restoration of RPE tight junctions is thus a plausible biomarker for therapeutic efficacy.  

Previous Use  
• Mandal et al. (Sci. Rep. 2017) used high-content imaging of ZO-1 continuity in ARPE-19 cells under oxidative challenge to screen a small antioxidant library; they identified N-acetylcysteine amide as a partial barrier rescuer.  
• Chang et al. (J Biomol Screen 2018) adapted the same tight-junction readout to a 384-well format, screening ~3,000 bioactive compounds.  They discovered that selective ROCK inhibitors not only restored occludin localization but also normalized TEER in stressed RPE.  
• In parallel, academic groups have correlated in vitro tight-junction rescue with in vivo rodent models: compounds that improved ZO-1 continuity in culture also reduced RPE leakage and subretinal fluid accumulation in sodium iodate–injured rats (Smith et al., Exp Eye Res. 2019).  
• Although no tight-junction–targeting therapeutic has yet advanced to late-stage dry AMD trials, these pioneering studies validate the assay’s ability to identify barrier-rescuing agents.  

Overall Evaluation  

Strengths  
• Directly measures a central, early hallmark of dry AMD (RPE barrier dysfunction) rather than downstream cell death.  
• Quantitative, high-content readout amenable to medium-throughput screening of large compound sets.  
• Compatible with human cells (primary or iPSC-derived), increasing translational relevance.  
• Image-based metrics (junction continuity, intensity) can be multiplexed with cell-viability or oxidative-stress probes in the same well.  

Weaknesses  
• RPE monolayer in 2D does not fully recapitulate Bruch’s membrane interactions, drusen buildup, or choroidal endothelial cross-talk.  
• ARPE-19 lines may differ from native RPE in tight-junction protein expression and response to stress; use of primary or iPSC-RPE increases realism but also cost and variability.  
• The assay models only barrier aspects—not photoreceptor phagocytosis, lipid handling, or complement regulation—so hits will require orthogonal validation in multi-cellular co-cultures or organoids.  
• High-content imaging infrastructure and image-analysis expertise are prerequisites, raising the technical barrier for some labs.  

Conclusion  
The Tight-Junction Imaging Assay is a well-validated, disease-relevant in vitro platform for identifying agents that restore RPE barrier integrity—a key step in dry AMD pathogenesis.  While it does not capture all facets of the disease, it provides a highly quantitative, human-cell–based screening tool that can de-risk early-stage compounds before moving into more complex co-culture systems or in vivo models.', 'index': '11'}

On the basal side, researchers deposit liposome–complement–hydroxyapatite particles that mimic the lipid-protein mineral composition of native drusen.
